Phillis Wheatley. Around 1753 to 1784, an enslaved African-American poet who became the first Black person and one of the first women to publish a book in the American colonies. Her work, composed while enslaved in Boston, demonstrated intellectual prowess and challenged prevailing assumptions about African inferiority and women's literary capacity.

Wheatley published Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral in 1773 while enslaved, making her the first African-American and first Black woman to publish a book in North America. Her poems addressed George Washington, the Earl of Dartmouth, and other prominent figures, establishing her as an intellectual voice during the Revolutionary era. She wrote in the neoclassical style of the eighteenth century, employing classical allusions, Christian themes, and formal verse structures that demonstrated mastery of the literary establishment's conventions.

Wheatley was owned by Boston merchant John Wheatley, who recognized her talent and allowed her education, a decision that was highly unusual and was contested by many who questioned whether Africans were even capable of intellectual achievement. Though constrained by her position and the literary conventions of her time, she addressed slavery obliquely in her work. Yet her very existence as a published poet was a refutation of racist ideology.

Wheatley lived briefly in freedom after manumission but died in poverty at thirty, and her legacy was obscured for generations before being recovered by African-American literary historians. She established the lineage that later poets like Langston Hughes would extend and transform, proving that intellectual authority belonged to Black writers from the very birth of American letters.
